🇮🇩   Mini and Micro LNG – an Indonesian example….

Here is a great example of what entrepreneurs can and will undertake when they have practical access to LNG, i.e. #LNG #infrastructure that can make bulk/wholesale LNG available for sale on small scale, mini or micro basis.

PT National Energy Solutions and PT Laras Ngarso Gede (Laras Energy), along withPT ITDC Nusantara Utilitas (ITDC Utilities), completed in march 2025 the last mile solution for an#ssLNG project to bring natural gas to Nusa Dua, Bali.

The consortium called “KSO NES-LARAS”  operates its own independent gas infrastructure completely inside The Nusa Dua resort enclave consisting of micro-LNG#regasification facilities and an 8.5 km local#gas #distribution network to dozens of commercial hotels and resorts in the resort enclave.

In addition, Laras Energy also delivers LNG via#ISO tanks and cylinders to local hospitality and horeca businesses in Bali to replace higher-emission#LPG and#diesel and become the first company that provides Mini- and micro-LNG solutions or#CNG distribution solutions for micro to medium consumer as a clean and safe energy.

As shown in the photo’s below, LNG is even delivered in standard portable cryogenic liquid cylinder (often referred to as a#Dewar cylinder, Dura-Cyl or VGL) used for transport and storage of liquefied gases like LNG.  They are supplied in various sizes e.g. from 170 to 220 liters and the larger class of 400 to 500 liters, whilst only 1.70 to 1.9m tall.

For now, to feed this mini R-LNG distribution network, the LNG ISO containers are sourced from Pasuruan micro-LNG plant in East Java  and are delivered to Bali rather than being loaded or sourced from the Benoa LNG Terminal (the Tanjung Benoa FSRU in Benoa Port, Bali) which is dedicated to supply upto 50 mmscfd to the 200 MW dual-fuel Pesanggaran Power Plant about 4 km away.

It will be interesting to watch if sourcing optimisation, swaps and back-filling will become part of the ssLNG landscape in#Indonesia in general and#Bali in particular.

Nevertheless, it is exciting to see that mini- and micro-LNG developments are becoming common practice in Indonesia which will become a self-fulling prophecy as one project will set the example for many others in the future and feed the spinning wheel of success and hopefully provide the motivation for the large scale LNG developers and projects to provide commercial and physical tie-ins through ssLNG/C, ISO loading bays and loading berths to support such initiatives in the country and the region.

Andy Herawan

INDONESIANS CAN WORK IN SINGAPORE — WITHOUT S PASS OR EP. 

How?

Through the Singapore–Indonesia Tech:X Programme, a bilateral initiative that allows eligible young professionals from Singapore and Indonesia to undertake work stints of up to ONE YEAR in each other's markets. It's not a visa-free arrangement. It's a dedicated Tech:X Pass pathway, designed specifically for young talent in technology and innovation.

And I think there's something much bigger behind this programme.

This is a collaboration between two governments that recognises something important: the future of economic growth is not just about where businesses operate, but also where they find, develop and exchange talent.

Singapore has a strong ecosystem for technology, innovation, capital and international business. Indonesia, on the other hand, has a huge domestic market, a growing digital economy and an increasingly important pool of young talent.

An Indonesian software engineer gets the opportunity to work with a Singapore technology company, gain international exposure and understand how businesses operate in a different market.

A Singapore tech company gets someone who understands Indonesia's culture, consumers and business environment before making its next expansion move.

A young Singaporean gets the opportunity to experience Indonesia firsthand, build regional connections and develop a better understanding of one of Southeast Asia's largest economies.

To me, this is how regional integration should look in practice.

I see three long-term opportunities coming out of this:

1. For businesses: A more practical way to test cross-border opportunities, build local capabilities and develop talent before committing to a bigger regional expansion.

2. For young professionals: An opportunity to gain international exposure, develop cross-cultural experience and become future leaders who understand both markets.

3. For Singapore and Indonesia: Stronger people-to-people connections, knowledge exchange and a more integrated regional talent ecosystem.

I believe the next generation of business leaders in Southeast Asia will not be defined by which country they come from, but by how well they understand and navigate different markets. And programmes like Tech:X could be one of the stepping stones towards that future.

Young engineers often ask me: "Which code do I use?" 
Simple answer: it depends on what you are welding.

𝘼𝙎𝙈𝙀 𝙄𝙓: how to qualify. WPS, PQR, welder tests. It does not tell you if a production weld is acceptable. Your construction code does. I learned this writing my first 10+ ASME/PED WPS at Tetra Pak on Year 2003.
𝘼𝙎𝙈𝙀 𝘽31.3: process piping inside the plant. Normal Fluid Service needs at least 5% random RT or UT (341.4.1). Hydrotest not less than 1.5 times design pressure (345.4.2).
𝘼𝙋𝙄 1104: pipeline girth welds. NDT acceptance is set by defect length (Section 9), not only defect type.

The mistake I see most: using one code's acceptance criteria on another code's job. Check the contract first.
Save this for your next project.
Which code do you open most in your job?

𝑲𝒉𝒐𝒊𝒓𝒊 𝑨𝒍𝒊, 𝑺𝑻., 𝑴𝑴., 𝑰𝑾𝑬.

“Careers are not linear.”

That’s what LinkedIn’s Trisha Suresh said during an ASEAN Ahead AI Career Readiness session in Singapore yesterday, and it stayed with me.

Even when you run a programme, you still leave a room like that with things to think about. Her points on how quickly skills for the same role can change, why AI literacy needs to be mainstream for everyone (not just engineers), and the value of the human skills that take longer to build all landed.

Thank you toJeslin Bay, Paddy Tan, Jessica Wong and the teams fromBlackStorm Group, Singapore Polytechnic, and Institute of Technical Education. A few students stayed back not only to talk about CVs and interviews, but to ask how The ASEAN Secretariat and theASEAN Foundation actually work. Those questions are part of why these sessions matter.

Still thinking about it on the way back to Jakarta.
